introduction: Paired escalators frame a multi-level retail atrium. Their champagne-bronze metal casings follow the incline and turn around rounded end pods, with flutes running across the double-curved undersides. This fabrication record covers the architectural casing. The photographs follow the work from bare formed panels through full-scale fit-up on steel rigs to the installed escalator runs.

sections.title: Architectural Casing for Paired Atrium Escalators
paragraphs: The metal scope comprises the inclined underside skins, rounded end pods and surrounding smooth fascia. The mirrored escalator arrangement puts the slopes and fluting in the same sightline, so the main curves and edge transitions read as one architectural element from the atrium floor.

sections.title: Keeping the Flute Pattern Through a Double Curve
paragraphs: At the rounded pod, the ribs turn through a changing radius while terminating against a smooth band. From below, local ripples, stepped seams and changes in finish direction are easy to see because the underside catches long bands of reflected light.

points.title: Forming the rib field
points.text: On a double curve, the rib geometry and the folded perimeter have to be developed together. A change at the return can shift where the visible rib ends land.

points.title: Rib-to-fascia alignment
points.text: The rounded nose brings smooth metal and multiple flutes into one sightline. The break line should read continuously from both the side and the underside.

points.title: Finish direction
points.text: Adjacent champagne-bronze panels must be assessed together under the intended viewing angles. Direction changes are most apparent where broad fluted faces pick up raking light.

sections.title: Forming the Fluted Skins and Pod Transitions
paragraphs: At the bench, the bare fluted skin shows the relationship between its rib field and the continuous folded edge. The unfinished pod exposes the joints and the smooth areas that frame the curved ribs. These views make the panel geometry visible before the champagne-bronze finish draws the surfaces together.

sections.title: Full-Scale Fit-Up on Steel Rigs
paragraphs: The workshop rig raises the casing so the team can see the same underside that visitors will see from below. Viewed along the incline and at the nose, the fitted modules show how the flutes carry across long runs and converge at the end pods. Separate pods on stands provide a closer view of the side profile and nose transitions.

paragraphs: The installed views trace the cladding from the paired lower-level approach to the stacked runs above. The close view across the atrium void shows the curved nose from below, where the rib field turns into the smooth perimeter just beneath the glass guard.

sections.title: What to Specify for a Fluted Escalator Casing
paragraphs: Coordinate the casing geometry with the escalator supplier’s envelope and the architect’s finished floor and ceiling lines before fixing module seams.

points.title: Drawings
points.text: Supply coordinated CAD or dimensioned PDFs with the escalator envelope, section datums, inclined run, end-pod geometry and required service clearances.

points.title: Samples
points.text: Review a curved sample with the actual rib spacing, end transition and proposed champagne-bronze finish under representative lighting.

points.title: Handling
points.text: Confirm the maximum shipping and site access envelope, lifting route and practical module split. Agree a numbering plan with the installer before packing.

conclusion: The photographs show why fluted escalator cladding needs to be reviewed from below as well as in elevation. On a similar atrium project, send the escalator supplier’s CAD or PDF envelope, the architectural sections and the proposed finish direction so the panel breaks, pod geometry and full-scale fit-up can be scoped together.
